client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it — all I can think about is that she's not there, and it makes the whole thing feel hollow and sad. I'm honestly not sure if talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds really heavy — grief has a way of casting a shadow over moments that used to feel joyful, and that sense of hollowness at family gatherings makes so much sense. I also notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's a kind of exhaustion underneath your words, like you've been holding this for a while and part of you isn't sure you have the energy left to hope that talking will help. What would it mean for you if this *did* help — is there a part of you that wants to believe it could?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there is a part of me that wants to believe it could help, but it feels almost dangerous to hope for that. Like if I let myself think things could get better and then they don't, I'll just feel worse than I already do. It's easier to just keep my expectations low and get through each day without thinking too far ahead.
therapist: That fear of hope is so real — it's actually a very common way our minds try to protect us from more pain, especially when we're already hurting. What you're describing, keeping expectations low as a kind of shield, makes a lot of sense as a coping strategy, even if it also means keeping yourself at arm's length from any relief. I'm curious — has there been a time in your life before this loss where letting yourself hope for something actually worked out, even in a small way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there have been small moments like that. I remember hoping my friend would show up to my birthday a few years back when things were rough between us, and she actually did, and it felt really good for a while. But then we drifted apart anyway, so even that kind of proves my point, doesn't it? Like, hope just delays the hurt.
therapist: It's really interesting that when you recalled your friend showing up, there was something almost warm in the way you described it — like that memory still carries some meaning, even as your mind quickly moved to reframe it as proof that hope fails. I wonder if it's possible that both things are true at once: that the good moment *was* real and valuable, and that the pain of drifting apart was also real — rather than the second part canceling out the first. What do you think it would feel like to let that birthday memory just be a good thing, without it needing to serve as evidence for or against anything?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me wants to just agree because it sounds nice. But when I actually try to sit with that memory as just... a good thing, my brain immediately goes to "okay but then what happened after," like I can't let it stand on its own without bracing for the fall. It feels almost dangerous to let myself feel good about it, like I'd be setting myself up to get hurt again.
therapist: What you're describing — that automatic bracing, the mind jumping ahead to protect you before you've even finished feeling something good — is such a telling pattern, and it sounds exhausting to live inside of. It's almost like your brain has become a very vigilant guard dog, so trained to watch for danger that it won't even let you rest in a safe moment. I'm curious, when you were just talking about that memory right now, did any part of you — even briefly — actually feel something good before the "but then" kicked in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think... maybe for like a second there was something. When I was describing that moment with my friends at the lake, there was this tiny flicker of warmth before my brain went straight to "that was the last time things felt normal." It's so brief that I almost wonder if I'm just imagining it, or if I'm only noticing it now because you asked.
therapist: That flicker is real — you noticed it, and I noticed something in the way you described it too, like there was a quiet tenderness there even as your words tried to talk you out of it. You don't have to be certain whether it's "real enough" or not; the fact that it was there at all, even for a second, is actually really significant. What if that brief warmth isn't a trick your mind is playing on you, but rather a small piece of evidence that some part of you still knows how to feel something good?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do. But it's hard not to wonder if that warmth is just... I don't know, some kind of muscle memory from before everything fell apart, not something that actually belongs to who I am now. Like maybe I'm just borrowing a feeling that doesn't really fit me anymore.
therapist: The way you just said that — softly, almost carefully — felt like someone handling something fragile, and I wonder if that fragility is actually a sign that this warmth *does* belong to you, not that it doesn't. Grief can make us feel like we've become a different person, like the "before" self and the "after" self are strangers, but what if the part of you that felt that flicker isn't borrowed from the past — what if it's been quietly surviving alongside all the pain? I'm curious, when you imagine "who you are now," what does that person look like to you — is there any room in that picture for someone who is both hurting *and* still capable of warmth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when I picture who I am now, I mostly see someone who's just... getting through the day, you know? Like someone who's functional on the outside but kind of hollow in the middle. I want to believe there's room for both the hurting and the warmth, but honestly it feels a little like wishful thinking when most days I'm just trying not to feel like a burden to the few people I have left.
therapist: That image of being functional on the outside but hollow in the middle is so vivid, and I want to gently stay with something you said at the end — that you're trying not to feel like a burden to the people you have left. That's a really important thing to have shared, and I want to make sure I understand it — when that feeling of being a burden shows up, what does it tell you about how you see yourself in relation to the people who care about you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when that feeling shows up, it tells me that I'm more of a weight than a presence in people's lives. Like, they'd probably be relieved if I just... needed less, you know? It's this constant background hum that whatever I bring to a relationship is mostly just problems and emotional labor for the other person.
therapist: That "background hum" you're describing — the constant quiet voice telling you that you're a weight rather than a presence — sounds like it's been running for a long time, maybe even before your grandmother passed. I want to gently push back on something, though: the fact that you're here, trying to understand yourself, being this thoughtful and honest, that *is* something you're bringing to the people in your life, not just problems. I'm wondering — is there anyone in your life who has actually told you, in their own words, that you're too much, or is this mostly a story your mind has constructed to protect them from something it's decided they can't handle?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, no one has ever said it to me directly — not in those words. But I think that almost makes it worse, because then I can't point to a moment and say "that's where this came from," it just feels like something I've always known, like gravity. And when you say I'm bringing something to people by being here and being thoughtful... I hear you, but part of me wonders if that's just something therapists are trained to say.
therapist: That instinct to question whether I mean it — that's not cynicism, that's actually a really honest and self-aware thing to notice, and I'd rather you push back on me than just accept what I say to feel better in the moment. But I'm also noticing that even as your words were measured and thoughtful just now, there was something that felt a little rushed, almost like you were trying to get through what you were saying before you could feel too much of it — does that resonate at all? And I'm curious about this feeling you described as "something I've always known, like gravity" — I wonder what it would mean for you if that certainty turned out to be something you *learned* rather than something that's simply true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that I was rushing through it — like if I said it fast enough, I could just report it without actually sitting in it. It's easier to describe the feeling from a distance than to actually let it land. And the thing about it being learned rather than just true... that's uncomfortable, because if it's something I picked up somewhere, that almost makes it worse, like I let something false become the foundation of how I see myself.
therapist: The discomfort you're feeling makes complete sense, but I want to gently offer a reframe: discovering that something is learned isn't a sign that you failed or "let" it happen — it actually means it isn't carved into who you are, it means it had a beginning, which means it can have a different ending too. You noticed just now that you were rushing to stay at a distance from your own feelings, and then you *stopped* and actually let that land a little — that's not a small thing. What would it feel like to hold the possibility that unlearning something, even something that's felt like gravity, might be something you're already, slowly, starting to do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
